identity.title: Food Safety Plan for Ready-to-Eat Hummus and Bean Dips

scan.summary: This is the required written food safety plan under FDA's FSMA Preventive Controls rule (21 CFR 117.126) for the production of refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips at the Salem plant. The plan documents the facility's hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, supply-chain requirements, and training for a product with a 45-day refrigerated shelf life made from cooked beans, tahini, spices, and oils. The plan identifies and controls for vegetative pathogens, spore-forming bacteria, Listeria monocytogenes, sesame allergen, and metal contamination.
scan.freshness_note: The plan is effective as of May 12, 2025 and is recent. However, it was prepared over 16 months ago and should be reviewed for any changes in operations, ingredients, or regulations since that date. No evidence of reanalysis per 21 CFR 117.170 has been provided.

gaps.title: Missing recall plan
gaps.description: 21 CFR 117.139 requires a written recall plan whenever a hazard requiring a preventive control is identified. This plan identifies six hazards requiring preventive controls (vegetative pathogens, spore-formers, Listeria, sesame allergen, and metal) but does not include a written recall plan with procedures for notifying customers, removing product from distribution, and destroying or reworking affected lots.
gaps.fix: Add a section describing the recall procedure, including identification of affected products, customer notification protocol, distribution tracking, removal procedures, and effectiveness verification. This must be documented before any incident occurs.
gaps.quote: No recall plan section is present in the submitted document

gaps.title: Missing signed approval by owner or operator
gaps.description: 21 CFR 117.310 requires that the owner, operator, or agent in charge of the facility must sign and date the food safety plan. The document shows approval by 'Plant Manager' but does not show a signature, date, or explicit identification that this person is the owner or agent in charge of the facility.
gaps.fix: Obtain a signed and dated approval from the owner or agent in charge of the facility (not just the plant manager) with their title and date clearly shown. This must be retained as required by 21 CFR 117.310.

gaps.title: Vague corrective action for positive Listeria environmental swabs
gaps.description: Section 6 states that if a Listeria spp. swab is positive, product made since the last negative swab is held pending investigation, but does not specify what 'investigation' means, how long product is held, how many repeat swabs trigger a determination, or when product is released or discarded. This creates ambiguity in execution and record-keeping.
gaps.fix: Clarify the investigation protocol: specify the number and location of additional swabs required, the decision rule for release versus discard (e.g., two consecutive negatives, or alternative corrective action), the maximum hold time, and which roles make the release decision. Document in the corrective action log.
gaps.locator: section 6, paragraph on Listeria spp. swabs
gaps.quote: If a Listeria spp. swab is positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since the last negative swab is held pending investigation.

gaps.title: No evidence of shelf-life studies for Listeria control
gaps.description: The plan relies on a 45-day refrigerated shelf life and monthly testing for Listeria monocytogenes in finished product to verify control of this hazard, but does not document that this shelf life was validated by challenge testing or durability studies. For a ready-to-eat product that can support Listeria growth, this validation is necessary to demonstrate that the product meets regulatory requirements (whether under FDA jurisdiction or if exported to EU markets that have stricter requirements effective July 2026).
gaps.fix: Conduct or obtain a formal shelf-life study (challenge test per EN ISO 20976-1 or equivalent) demonstrating that Listeria monocytogenes will not exceed safe limits throughout the 45-day shelf life under normal refrigeration. Document the study results, test parameters, and acceptance criteria. Retain this in the food safety plan file.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.155(b) (validation of process controls); also EU Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Annex for imported product
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: Incomplete sanitation monitoring locations and frequency
gaps.description: Section 5 states that the sanitation lead records ATP swab results 'before each start-up' and section 4 specifies 'ATP swab pass before start-up; Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2.' However, the frequency of ATP swabs (daily? per product change?) is not clarified, and the specific locations of the 10 sites are not mapped or identified in the document. Without clear location identification, there is risk of inconsistent monitoring.
gaps.fix: Add an attachment or detailed section identifying the exact 10 locations by equipment name, area, or map coordinates. Clarify ATP swab frequency (e.g., 'before each production run' or 'daily at start-up'). Define what constitutes 'zone 1 and 2' (direct food-contact surfaces, adjacent surfaces, etc.) and confirm this aligns with 21 CFR 117.95.
gaps.quote: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

gaps.title: No calibration schedule or tolerance for metal detector
gaps.description: Section 4 specifies metal detector test piece rejection thresholds (2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm nonferrous, 3.0 mm stainless) and section 7 states the detector is 'serviced by the manufacturer annually,' but the plan does not specify the frequency of detector sensitivity verification between annual services, acceptance/rejection criteria for test runs, or what happens if sensitivity drifts. The current language requires test pieces at start-up and every two hours, but does not specify whether the detector must pass or be recalibrated if a test fails.
gaps.fix: Add a table or procedure specifying: (1) frequency of detector calibration (e.g., per manufacturer recommendations); (2) acceptance criteria for test piece runs (must pass all three sizes or percentage pass); (3) action if a test piece fails (stop production, recalibrate, re-run product); (4) maintenance/cleaning frequency; (5) retention of calibration records. This should reference the detector manual and the manufacturer's specifications.
gaps.quote: the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually

gaps.title: Probe thermometer calibration method may not be sufficient
gaps.description: Section 7 states probe thermometers are 'calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,' which is a two-point calibration. For a critical control point that governs the kill step (212°F for 60 minutes), a two-point calibration may not be adequate to verify accuracy across the full operating range, especially near 212°F. NIST and FDA guidance often recommends three-point calibration or certified calibration reference.
gaps.fix: Upgrade the calibration procedure to include a three-point calibration (ice water at 32°F, boiling water at 212°F, and a mid-range reference point such as a certified water bath at 140°F or 180°F) or use a NIST-traceable calibrator. Document the results and tolerance (±1°F or ±0.5°C) in the plan and in the verification records. Retain certificates of calibration for all probes.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.145(b) (monitoring requirements); FDA Compliance Program Guidance (CPG 545.450, metal detectors) and NIST SP 250 guidance on thermometer calibration
gaps.quote: Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly

gaps.title: Insufficient documented risk-based justification for hazard exclusions
gaps.description: The hazard analysis table (section 3) lists 'Date coding' with 'None significant — No' and no justification. While date coding itself may not be a hazard, the hazard analysis should document why this step does not introduce or allow any pathogens or allergens to proliferate or persist. Additionally, the 'blending and filling' step hazard focuses only on Listeria but does not explicitly address whether sesame allergen cross-contact occurs at this step (it is controlled only at product scheduling and washdown).
gaps.fix: Expand the justification for date coding (e.g., 'Date coding is a cold, non-contact step; no hazard identified'). Clarify under 'Blending and filling' whether sesame cross-contact is a hazard at this step and if not, explain why (e.g., sesame is added only in labeled products, blending occurs before sesame addition, or washdown between products prevents cross-contact). This supports 21 CFR 117.130(b).
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.130(b)(1) (hazard analysis must consider biological, chemical, and physical hazards)

gaps.title: No documented method for allergen label review at printing
gaps.description: Section 4 states 'Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in the day, followed by full washdown.' However, section 5 states only 'The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.' There is no documented procedure for label review at the printing stage, nor is there a log entry or record requirement for that review. This creates a gap in execution and verification of the allergen control.
gaps.fix: Add a specific procedure for label review at printing: specify who performs it (quality technician?), when in the printing process, what documents are consulted (formulation sheet, printing order, SKU list), and what to do if a mismatch is found (e.g., halt printing, quarantine labels, rework). Require a signature and date in the label log for printing-stage review.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.135(b) (preventive controls must include measures such as label reviews); 21 CFR 117.145(a) (monitoring the implementation of preventive controls)
gaps.quote: Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in the day, followed by full washdown

gaps.title: Missing blast chiller performance specification and validation
gaps.description: The cooling process critical limit is '135°F to 70°F in 2 hours; 70°F to 41°F in 4 hours' using a 'blast chiller,' but the plan does not specify the chiller model, capacity, or whether it has been validated to meet this time/temperature profile. If the blast chiller is undersized or malfunctions, cooling times may exceed limits, yet there is no corrective action procedure that addresses chiller repair or replacement.
gaps.fix: Add to section 4 (Preventive controls): the model and capacity of the blast chiller, reference to a validation study showing it achieves the time/temperature profile under typical product loads, and a corrective action in section 6 for cooling delays (e.g., 'If cooling exceeds time limits: discard batch. If chiller malfunction is suspected, service the chiller per manufacturer and re-validate performance before resuming production').
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1) (critical limits must be established); 21 CFR 117.155(b) (validation of process controls)
gaps.quote: Cool cooked beans from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller

scan.confidence_notes: Confidence is high that this document is a food safety plan prepared under FSMA (21 CFR 117.126) and that the major sections (hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, supply-chain, records, training) are present and generally compliant with the rule structure. However, several significant gaps exist: (1) the written recall plan is missing entirely, which is a mandatory element; (2) the food safety plan is not signed by the owner or agent in charge, as required by 21 CFR 117.310; (3) critical limits and monitoring procedures lack precision (e.g., Listeria investigation protocol, exact sanitation swab locations, metal detector calibration tolerance); (4) there is no evidence of shelf-life validation studies for Listeria control, which is necessary for a 45-day refrigerated ready-to-eat product capable of supporting growth of this pathogen; (5) the thermometer calibration method (two-point, ice and boiling water) is below the recommended standard for a critical control point at 212°F. The plan demonstrates competent hazard analysis and reasonable preventive control strategy, but implementation and documentation require improvement. Confidence is medium-to-high on the existence of gaps but lower on whether all performance monitoring and corrective actions are being executed consistently in the field—this would be verified only by inspection or audit of the actual monitoring and corrective action logs.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.
3. Hazard analysis

4. Preventive controls

the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
